# Cat scratch disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Wound, soft tissue, bone, and joint infections > Cat scratch disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/IF0Yj3)

---

## Summary

Cat scratch disease (CSD) is a typically <u>self-limited</u> infectious disease that predominantly affects children and <u>adolescents</u>. It is caused by <u>Bartonella henselae</u>, a gram-negative, aerobic <u>bacillus</u>, which is transmitted via animal (most commonly cat) bites, scratches, or saliva exposure. CSD is typically localized and manifests with ≥ 1 <u>erythematous</u> nontender <u>papule</u> and/or <u>pustule</u> at the cutaneous site of <u>inoculation</u>, followed by painful <u>proximal</u> <u>lymphadenopathy</u>. <u>Extranodal CSD</u> (e.g., ocular involvement, <u>encephalitis</u>, culture-negative <u>endocarditis</u>) is rare, but <u>immunocompromised</u> patients are at increased risk for extranodal involvement and severe infection (e.g., <u>bacillary angiomatosis</u> or <u>bacillary peliosis</u>). Diagnosis is typically clinical but can be confirmed with <u>laboratory studies</u> (e.g., <u>serology</u>). <u>Localized CSD</u> in immunocompetent patients typically resolves within 6 months without treatment, although <u>azithromycin</u> may be used to reduce <u>lymphadenopathy</u> and disease duration. Specialist consultation is recommended for <u>immunocompromised</u> patients and those with extranodal disease. Prevention involves regular cat <u>flea</u> treatment, avoiding scratches and bites, and immediately washing any injuries with soap and water.




<u>Bacillary angiomatosis</u> is covered in more detail in a separate article.

---

## Epidemiology

Predominantly affects children and <u>adolescents</u>



Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: : <u>B. henselae</u> (gram-negative, aerobic <u>bacillus</u>)

* Transmission

* Infection is spread from animal to animal via <u>flea</u> bites. [[1]](/library/Bedza60)

* Human <u>inoculation</u>

* Primarily occurs via animal (most commonly cat) scratches, bites, and saliva exposure

* Rarely transmitted via <u>flea</u> bites [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)

* Kittens are more likely to infect humans than older cats.  [[1]](/library/Bedza60)

---

## Clinical features

### Localized CSD [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)




Uncomplicated localized disease occurs in 85–90% of patients with CSD and includes the following:




* ≥ 1 <u>papule</u> and/or <u>pustule</u> at the cutaneous site of <u>inoculation</u>

* 5–10 mm, <u>erythematous</u>, nontender

* Typically manifests 3–12 days after exposure

* Regional <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* Swollen, tender <u>lymph nodes</u> 7–60 days after exposure

* Usually unilateral

* Most commonly involves <u>lymph nodes</u> <u>proximal</u> to the site of exposure in the <u>axilla</u>, neck, or groin

* Occasionally suppurate

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>: <u>fever</u> (may be prolonged), <u>malaise</u>, <u>myalgias</u>, loss of appetite [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[4]](/library/K3dUjp0)

### Extranodal CSD [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)




Up to 15% of patients develop extranodal disease due to <u>autoinoculation</u> (e.g., in ocular involvement) or hematogenous spread. [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)




* Ocular involvement (occurs in up to 10% of patients) [[1]](/library/Bedza60)

* Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome: unilateral follicular <u>conjunctivitis</u> and tender <u>ipsilateral</u> preauricular <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* Neuroretinitis: sudden, unilateral, painless <u>vision loss</u>; <u>optic nerve</u> <u>edema</u>; star-shaped macular <u>exudates</u>

* <u>Bacillary angiomatosis</u> [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)

* Multiple red-purple <u>papules</u> that bleed easily

* See “<u>Symptoms of bacillary angiomatosis</u>” for more information.

* Bacillary peliosis [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[5]](/library/x3dEkp0)

* A rare vascular condition characterized by multiple blood-filled cysts and vascular sinuses in the <u>liver</u>

* Often detected incidentally on imaging

* Symptoms (if present) include abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, weight loss, <u>jaundice</u>, <u>hepatomegaly</u>, and, rarely, <u>hemorrhagic shock</u>.

* Additional manifestations include: [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[6]](/library/Xmd9Vq0)

* Culture-negative <u>endocarditis</u> [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/x3dEkp0)

* <u>Encephalitis</u>  [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)

* <u>Osteomyelitis</u>

* <u>Pneumonia</u>

* <u>Glomerulonephritis</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Bacillary angiomatosis</u> and <u>bacillary peliosis</u> predominantly affect <u>immunocompromised</u> patients (e.g., patients with <u>HIV</u> and <u>CD4<sup>+</sup> count</u> < 100/mmÂ³). [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[4]](/library/K3dUjp0)

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)




* <u>Localized cat scratch disease</u> can be <u>diagnosed clinically</u> if the patient has:

* Characteristic features of <u>localized CSD</u>

* Relevant history of exposure to cats

* Extranodal disease or diagnostic uncertainty: Confirm the diagnosis with <u>serology</u> and/or advanced studies.





### <u>Serology</u> [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)




* Test: <u>Bartonella</u> spp. <u>IgG</u> and <u>IgM</u>

* Limitations

* <u>False negatives</u> in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients, e.g., <u>advanced HIV</u> [[7]](/library/SSdy_60)

* <u>False positives</u> from: [[1]](/library/Bedza60)

* Previous exposure

* Infection with other <u>Bartonella</u> spp., <u>Chlamydia pneumoniae</u>, or <u>Coxiella burnetii</u>

* Interpretation of results [[1]](/library/Bedza60)

* Positive: <u>IgM</u> positive or <u>IgG</u> <u>titer</u> ≥ 1:256 [[4]](/library/K3dUjp0)

* Inconclusive: <u>IgG</u> <u>titer</u> between 1:64 and 1:256

* Repeat the test in 2–4 weeks.

* A subsequent <u>IgG</u> <u>titer</u> ≥ 1:256 or a fourfold increase from initial testing confirms the diagnosis. [[1]](/library/Bedza60)

* Negative: <u>IgG</u> <u>titer</u> < 1:64 [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)





### Advanced testing




The following studies are performed in diagnostic uncertainty, persistent symptoms, extranodal disease, and <u>immunocompromised</u> patients. [[7]](/library/SSdy_60)[[8]](/library/l4dvjJ0)




* <u>Blood cultures</u>  [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* <u>Biopsy</u> of <u>lymph node</u> or affected tissue and further studies (e.g. <u>histopathology</u> and/or <u>PCR</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Diagnostic testing may help confirm the diagnosis but cannot rule out <u>B. henselae</u> infection. [[2]](/library/j3d_Rp0)[[4]](/library/K3dUjp0)

---

## Pathology

* Warthin-Starry staining of the involved <u>lymph node</u> may show <u>clusters</u> of rod-shaped bacteria.

* H&E staining of cutaneous lesions may show necrotizing <u>granuloma</u> formation and neutrophilic infiltrate.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Kaposi sarcoma</u> has <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltrate as opposed to <u>bacillary angiomatosis</u>.

---

## Differential diagnoses

Consider other conditions associated with the following:




* Prolonged <u>fever</u>: <u>fever of unknown origin</u>

* <u>Skin</u> lesions

* <u>Kaposi sarcoma</u>

* <u>Pyogenic granuloma</u> [[7]](/library/SSdy_60)

* See also “<u>Differential diagnoses of bacillary angiomatosis</u>.”

* Regional <u>lymphadenopathy</u>: See “Localized <u>lymphadenopathy</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### <u>Localized CSD</u> [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)[[7]](/library/SSdy_60)




* Immunocompetent patients

* Treatment is not usually required as the infection is <u>self-limited</u> (resolves within 6 months) [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* Consider <u>azithromycin</u>  DOSAGE for 5 days to reduce <u>lymphadenopathy</u> and illness duration.  [[3]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* <u>Immunocompromised</u> patients

* Treatment is recommended for all <u>immunocompromised</u> patients.

* <u>Erythromycin</u> OR <u>doxycycline</u> (dosages are the same as for <u>treatment of bacillary angiomatosis</u>)  [[7]](/library/SSdy_60)

* Painful suppurative <u>lymph nodes</u>: Consider <u>aspiration</u> for symptom relief. [[1]](/library/Bedza60)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>incision and drainage</u> of suppurative <u>lymph nodes</u> due to the risk of <u>fistula</u> formation. [[1]](/library/Bedza60)




### <u>Extranodal CSD</u>




* Initiate management in consultation with appropriate specialists.

* <u>Antibiotics</u> are usually recommended.  [[9]](/library/tE1Xxi0)

* Commonly used regimes include: [[1]](/library/Bedza60)[[7]](/library/SSdy_60)

* <u>Erythromycin</u> OR <u>doxycycline</u>

* PLUS <u>rifampin</u> in patients with <u>endocarditis</u> or <u>CNS</u> involvement  [[5]](/library/x3dEkp0)

* See also “<u>Treatment of bacillary angiomatosis</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> The treatment course for extranodal disease is usually prolonged, and some <u>immunocompromised</u> patients may require long-term <u>suppressive antibiotic therapy</u>. [[7]](/library/SSdy_60)
